title: Ziegfeld's Show Girl and Maurice Chevalier's debut
summary: The band played the Ziegfeld show and Maurice Chevalier's American debut.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Do you think the Cotton Club shows were better than the Ziegfeld shows.

Oh, no. They're two different shows. Because Ziegfeld, he glamorized the American woman. We done a Ziegfeld show, next to the last show. 'Show Girl,' a show called 'Show Girl', with Ruby Keeler. Next to the last show he ever done, we were still at the Cotton Club and did that show. We were doubling that's right. The show 'Lives of an American in Paris', from the Ziegfeld shows, 'Liza', that all the bands played, was from that show. we played it. That's right. We were the first one of the (Unintelligible) to play a Ziegfeld show. Never had no colored band play it. We played it. That's right. Called 'Show Girl'. We did it for

12 or 13 weeks, we were doubling at the Cotton Club. We had an extra band to play till we got to the Cotton Club. We were the first band to play Maurice Chevalier at the Fulton Theatre. You know Maurice Chevalier. When he come to America, we played his debut at the Fulton Theatre on Broadway.
Did he choose the band, is that what he wanted or did somebody else come in?

It was done through our manager, Irvin Mills, connection. We played it. We played the first half of his show on stage, just us. No women was in the show. Us and the Barry Brothers, the famous Barry Brothers. That's a trio. No women in the show. We didn't take Ivie with us.

Ivie wasn't with us then, in the Cotton Club, Ethel Waters. No women. In the second part, when he come on, we played in the pit. Man, I remember opening night, Maurice Chevalier, you know, he's a Frenchman didn'tspeak no English at that time. Man, we opened with him, opened up the band and tore them down, then the Barry Brothers come out and tore them down.

We were on the stand playing and this cat was getting dressed to go, didn't have his pants on, just his shirt. No pants, he tried to run out on the stage, so much commotion in the audience. We were tearing them up, people screaming and hollering. He had never heard that. They had to hold that cat, man. He laughed at it when we saw him in Paris, when
we went to Europe in 1933, he laughed about it. He had been here and made some pictures, but we played his American debut. That's right. We had a lot of firsts.
